lessons.title: What Is Risk Parity? Equal Risk Contribution Explained

children.text: Chapter 1 left you one step short. Inverse-volatility weighting got the three-asset Nifty 50, G-Sec, and gold portfolio from a wildly uneven risk split to something close to even, roughly 33/31/36, but not exactly even, because it never looked at correlation. This lesson closes that last gap and gives risk parity its actual, formal definition.
The Formal Definition of Risk Parity

markDefs.definition: A portfolio construction rule that chooses weights so every asset contributes exactly the same share of total portfolio volatility, using the full covariance matrix including correlations.

children.text: , also called Equal Risk Contribution or ERC, is defined by a single condition: choose weights so that every asset's risk contribution, computed with the full covariance matrix from lesson 2 of the last chapter, is identical.

body.caption: The defining condition of risk parity. Every asset's risk contribution equals total portfolio volatility divided by the number of assets, exactly, not approximately.

body.text: Notice what is completely absent from that condition: expected returns. Risk parity's definition never mentions them. That is not an oversight, it is the entire point. Chapter 1 showed that mean-variance optimization amplifies small errors in return forecasts into large, unstable weight swings. A definition that never asks you to forecast a return cannot be destabilized by a bad return forecast, because there is nowhere for that forecast to enter the calculation.

children.text: The Two-Asset Case: A Clean Closed Form

With exactly two assets, the equal risk contribution condition simplifies beautifully. Setting RC1 equal to RC2 and expanding both sides using the MCTR formula from last chapter, every term involving the correlation and the pairwise covariance cancels out on both sides of the equation. What survives is strikingly simple.

body.caption: For exactly two assets, equal risk contribution reduces to w1*sigma1 = w2*sigma2. Correlation drops out of the equation entirely.

body.text: That ratio, w1/w2 = sigma2/sigma1, is exactly inverse-volatility weighting. For exactly two assets, risk parity and inverse-volatility weighting are the same portfolio, regardless of what the correlation between them is. This is why the 60/40 case study two lessons ago felt so intuitive to fix with inverse-vol weighting: with only two assets in the mix, inverse-vol weighting is not an approximation to risk parity, it is risk parity.

body.caption: Inverse-vol weights on the Nifty 50 / 10-year G-Sec pair (26.3% / 73.7%) give exactly equal risk contribution, no matter the correlation assumed

children.text: The portfolio's overall volatility moves around a lot as correlation changes, from 3.68% to 6.38% across this range, but the 50/50 risk split holds at every single value. That stability is exactly what a two-asset risk parity sleeve is supposed to deliver.
Three or More Assets: Why the Shortcut Breaks

The clean cancellation that happens with two assets does not happen with three or more. Set RC1 equal to RC2, and RC2 equal to RC3, and the covariance terms no longer cancel symmetrically, because each asset now has two correlation relationships pulling in potentially different directions instead of one. That is exactly why inverse-volatility weighting, which only ever looks at each asset's own volatility, landed close to but not exactly on equal risk contribution for the Nifty 50, G-Sec, and gold example: gold's positive correlation with equity and debt's negative correlation with equity pull their true risk contributions away from what their standalone volatility alone would predict.
Solving It: The Convex Optimization Trick

With three or more assets, equal risk contribution has to be solved numerically. Directly solving the system 'RC1 = RC2 = RC3' can be numerically awkward, the equations are nonlinear and there is no guarantee a naive solver converges cleanly. Florin Spinu's 2013 paper gave the field a much better route: reformulate the problem as a convex optimization, a type of problem numerical solvers handle reliably and are guaranteed to solve to a single, unique answer.

body.caption: Spinu's convex formulation of risk parity. The first term penalizes total portfolio variance, the second term (a log barrier) pushes every weight away from zero. Their balance point is exactly where every asset's unnormalized risk contribution is equal. Solve this, then rescale the resulting weights to sum to 1.

children.text: Why does this work? Take the derivative of that objective with respect to w_i and set it to zero: you get (Sigma w)_i = 1/(n * w_i), which rearranges to w_i * (Sigma w)_i = 1/n for every asset. That is precisely the unnormalized version of the equal risk contribution condition from the start of this lesson. The log barrier term is what forces the solver toward a strictly positive, balanced answer instead of the corner solutions that plagued unconstrained mean-variance optimization in chapter 1.
Case Study: Solving True Risk Parity for Nifty 50, G-Sec, and Gold

Run the same three-asset inputs from the end of chapter 1, equity volatility 14%, debt volatility 5%, gold volatility 12%, correlations of -0.10 (equity-debt), 0.05 (equity-gold), and 0.00 (debt-gold), through the convex solver. Here is how all three approaches compare, side by side, on the exact same inputs.

body.caption: 1/N vs inverse-volatility vs true risk parity: capital weights and risk contribution (illustrative)

body.title: Risk contribution share, all three schemes (illustrative)

body.text: Notice the direction of the small shifts from inverse-vol to true risk parity: debt's weight rises slightly, from 56.4% to 57.6%, while gold's falls slightly, from 23.5% to 22.2%. Debt's negative correlation with equity makes it an even better diversifier than its volatility alone suggests, so true risk parity rewards it with a bit more capital. Gold's mildly positive correlation with equity makes it a slightly weaker diversifier than its volatility alone suggests, so true risk parity trims its weight. Correlation is exactly what inverse-vol weighting was blind to.

body.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize  # pip install scipy

vol = np.array([0.14, 0.05, 0.12])  # Nifty 50, 10Y G-Sec, Gold (illustrative)
corr = np.array([
    [1.00, -0.10, 0.05],
    [-0.10, 1.00, 0.00],
    [0.05, 0.00, 1.00],
])
cov = np.outer(vol, vol) * corr
n = len(vol)

def spinu_objective(w, cov, n):
    return 0.5 * w @ cov @ w - (1 / n) * np.sum(np.log(w))

result = minimize(
    spinu_objective,
    x0=np.full(n, 1 / n),
    args=(cov, n),
    method='SLSQP',
    bounds=[(1e-6, None)] * n,
)

w_raw = result.x
w_erc = w_raw / w_raw.sum()  # rescale to sum to 1

port_vol = np.sqrt(w_erc @ cov @ w_erc)
mctr = (cov @ w_erc) / port_vol
rc_share = (w_erc * mctr) / port_vol

print('True risk parity weights:', np.round(w_erc * 100, 2))
print('Risk contribution shares:', np.round(rc_share * 100, 2))
print('Portfolio volatility:', f'{port_vol:.2%}')
body.caption: Swap in your own volatility and correlation estimates, built from real NSE, G-Sec, and gold ETF return series, and confirm the risk contribution shares come out equal to several decimal places, unlike inverse-vol weighting's approximate split.

body.title: Explaining the Shift to a Junior Analyst
body.scenario: A junior analyst on your desk sees the true risk parity solution give the 10-year G-Sec a larger weight (57.6%) than inverse-volatility weighting did (56.4%), and asks why the 'more accurate' method would put even more money into the least volatile asset in the portfolio.
body.prompt: How would you explain this without referring to expected returns anywhere in your answer?
body.modelAnswer: The extra weight has nothing to do with return forecasts, risk parity never uses any. It is entirely about diversification value. G-Secs are negatively correlated with equity, so they do more than just sit quietly at low volatility, they actively offset equity's swings and reduce total portfolio variance. Inverse-vol weighting only measures each asset's own standalone volatility and misses this offsetting effect completely. True risk parity's optimization sees the full covariance matrix, recognizes that debt is an even better risk-reducer than its volatility alone implies, and rewards it with a slightly larger allocation to keep every asset's risk contribution exactly equal.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: For a portfolio of exactly two assets, why does risk parity always produce the same weights as inverse-volatility weighting, regardless of the correlation between them?
options: Because with two assets, correlation is always assumed to be zero
Because expanding the equal risk contribution condition RC1 = RC2 for two assets causes every correlation-dependent term to cancel algebraically, leaving only w1*sigma1 = w2*sigma2
Because SEBI requires two-asset portfolios to be weighted by inverse volatility
Because two-asset portfolios cannot have a nonzero correlation by definition
body.explanation: The cancellation is a specific algebraic result of there being only one pairwise correlation term, and it appears identically in both RC1 and RC2, so it cancels when you set them equal. This convenient cancellation does not generalize to three or more assets, which is exactly why chapter 1's three-asset example needed a numerical solver to reach exact equal risk contribution.

body.text: Risk parity is the exact solution to the problem chapter 1 spent three lessons building up to: weights chosen so every asset's risk contribution, correlation included, is identical, without ever forecasting a return. For two assets it has a clean closed form that happens to equal inverse-volatility weighting. For three or more, it requires solving a convex optimization, but the payoff is a portfolio where no single asset can quietly dominate the risk budget.

points: Risk parity (Equal Risk Contribution, ERC) is defined purely in terms of risk: every asset's risk contribution must be identical. Expected returns never enter the definition at all.
For exactly two assets, the equal risk contribution condition collapses to w1*sigma1 = w2*sigma2, which is identical to inverse-volatility weighting, regardless of correlation.
For three or more assets, correlation terms no longer cancel symmetrically, so inverse-vol weighting only approximates equal risk contribution rather than achieving it exactly.

Spinu's (2013) convex reformulation, minimizing 0.5*w'Sigma*w minus a log-barrier term, solves the N-asset risk parity problem reliably, converging to a portfolio where a small, damped log barrier prevents any weight from collapsing toward zero.

On the Nifty 50, G-Sec, and gold example, true risk parity shifted weight slightly toward debt (a better diversifier than its volatility alone suggests, thanks to negative correlation with equity) and slightly away from gold (a slightly weaker diversifier, thanks to positive correlation with equity), landing on exactly equal 33.3% risk contribution for all three.
The next lesson turns this into a practical portfolio: building a real risk parity allocation using Nifty, G-Secs, and gold as the three sleeves.
